coredata.dc:description: Environmental pollution caused by plastic waste has become global problem that needs to be considered urgently. In the pursuit of a circular plastic economy, biodegradation provides an attractive strategy for managing plastic wastes, whereas effective plastic-degrading microbes and enzymes are required. In this study, we report that Blastobotrys sp. G-9 isolated from discarded plastic in landfills is capable of depolymerizing polyurethanes (PU) and poly (butylene adipate-co-terephthalate) (PBAT). Strain G-9 degrades up to 60% of PU foam after 21 days of incubation at 28 ℃ by breaking down carbonyl groups via secretory hydrolase as confirmed by structural characterization of plastics and degradation products identification. Within the supernatant of strain G-9, we identify a novel cutinase BaCut1, belonging to the esterase family, that can reproduce the same effect. BaCut1 demonstrates efficient degradation toward commercial polyester plastics PU foam (0.5 mg enzyme/25 mg plastic) and agricultural film PBAT (0.5 mg enzyme/10 mg plastic) with 50% and 18% weight loss at 37 ℃ for 48 h, respectively. BaCut1 hydrolyzes PU into adipic acid as a major end-product with 42.9% recovery via ester bond cleavage, and visible biodegradation is also identified from PBAT, which is a beneficial feature for future recycling economy. Molecular docking, along with products distribution, elucidates a special substrate-binding modes of BaCut1 with plastic substrate analogue. BaCut1-mediated polyester plastic degradation offers an alternative approach for managing PU plastic wastes through possible bio-recycling.

G-9 was isolated from the collected PUR plastic in landfills with the ability to adhere the plastic surface and decompose the polyurethanes (PUR) (Step 2). Strain G-9 secreted the cutinase BaCut1 and efficiently degraded the PUR and PBAT into adipic acid by a special substrate-binding mode (Step 3). BaCut1-mediated PUR degradation brings the alternative ways for PU plastic wastes management through bio-recycling, while how to realize the closed-loop waste PUR recycling process need to be further explored (Step 4). The step 1–4 indicate four major research ideas: step 1, PUR-degradative strain G-9 isolation; step 2, strain G-9 degrades PUR by cutinase Bacut1, step 3, Bacut1 degrades PUR into adipic acid by a special substrate binding model, step 4, future work need to be performed to elucidate the possible catalytic mechanism.

ce:section.ce:para: Plastic pollution is found globally in various habitats [1]. Out of the 8.3 billion tonnes of plastic produced so far, an estimated 6.3 billion tonnes had become waste by 2015. Of this amount, 12% was incinerated, 79% ended up in landfill sites or the natural environment, and only 9% was recycled [2]. Polyurethane (PU) accounts for 5.3% of global plastic production, while polybutylene adipate terephthalate (PBAT) represents 4.6% of the total global production capacities of bioplastics. These plastics are extensively used in the manufacture of furniture, automotive packaging, agricultural, medical and other sectors [3,4]. PBAT is a type of biodegradable polymer that is susceptible to enzymatic degradation due to the presence of the butylene adipate group. In contrast, PU primarily synthesized through the polyaddition of polyols and polyisocyanates, and its durable material properties ensure its continued presence. Typically, these materials are disposed through landfilling and incineration [5]. The accumulation of plastic waste on a large-scale has caused potential secondary pollution and significant wastage of carbon resources. Therefore, it is crucial to develop solutions to reduce or recycle wastes like PU and PBAT-like for their sustainable use.

Compared to traditional waste disposal methods, such as mechanical and chemical recycling, bio-based degradation and recycling techniques utilizing microbes or enzymes have emerged as promising strategies [3]. The biodegradation of polyethylene terephthalate (PET) with engineered cutinases has demonstrated the feasibility of a closed-loop waste plastic recycling process [6]. In recent years, numerous polyester plastic-degrading microbes, including Cladosporium, Bacillus, Pseudomonas, Cryptococcus, Comamonas and Staphylococcus, have been identified. These microbes secrete various hydrolases, such as esterases, cutinases, lipases, amidases ureases and proteases, capable of degrading PU or PBAT [3,7–9]. However, due to the internally cross-linked molecular properties that typically not accessible for depolymerization by biological means, most of the microbes and enzymes discovered to date exhibit limited efficiency in degrading PU plastics [3]. PU-degrading fungi have demonstrated efficient polymer degradation, with up to 80% weight loss observed from the degradation of PU foam by Cladosporium [10,11]. Additionally, Aspergillus flavus was also able to degrade 60% of PU film within 30 days [12]. Nevertheless, further exploration is required to identify the enzymes responsible for PU and PBAT decomposition.

Polyester PU consists of soft segments (long polyester- or polyether-based polyols) and organized hard segments (polyisocyanates). Enzymatic depolymerization of PU has primarily focused on poly(ester urethane), with hydrolases capable of accessing ester or amide bonds exhibiting potential PU-degrading ability. While most lipases operate at lipid-water interfaces facilitated by a mobile lid domain located over the active site [13,14], cutinases lack this lid structure, exposing an expansive substrate-binding conductive to productive catalysis [15]. Cutinases have shown high degradation efficiency toward polyester plastics, such as butylene succinate (PBS) [16], PET [17] and PBAT [15], offering potential for advancing PU biodegradation. Known enzymes like cutinases TtcutA [18], LCC, TfCut2 [19], Tcur1278 [20], HiC [21] act on PU by breaking ester-bonds. However, PU-degradation is not the primary function of most cutinases during enzyme evolution, and the identified PU-degrading enzymes commonly exhibit high activity on oligomers but low decomposition rates toward complex solid forms of most PU wastes [3,22].

Our work here commences with an initial observation of PU plastic degradation from landfills, where possible biodegradation was demonstrated by scanning electron microscope (SEM) and structural characterization. By developing a rapid screening method utilizing synthesized solid polyester-PU (PBA-PU) as the marker, we identified the fungal strain Blastobotrys sp. G-9 as the most effective degrader. Our findings reveal that strain G-9 can degrade PU foam through a newly identified cutinase, BaCut1, which converts PUR and PBAT into adipic acid as the major products. Intriguingly, BaCut1 exhibits no degradative activity toward PET. The identification of depolymerizing enzyme offers potential for industrial bio-recycling of PU and PBAT in the near future.

The pET-29a (+) vector (TaKaRa Biotechnology Co. Ltd., Dalian, China) was used to construct the recombinant expression plasmid. Escherichia coli DH5α and BL21 (DE3) were used for gene cloning and protein expression, respectively. Impranil® DLN-SD (an anionic aliphatic polyester polyurethane dispersion) was obtained from Covestro AG (Leverkusen, German). Poly(1,4-butylene adipate) (PBA, weight-average molecular weight (Mw)= 2000) and 4,4’-methylene diphenyl isocyanate (4,4’-MDI) were purchased from Aladdin Co., Ltd (Shanghai, China). Polyester PU foam was obtained from Dagong foam Co., Ltd (Nantong, China). The synthesis of PBA-PU was performed as described by Liu et al. [10]. Polyethylene terphthalate (PET) was purchased from Good Fellow (6–8% crystallinity) (England). Agricultural film PBAT (black) was donated from Henan Tianren biomaterials Research Institute Co., LTD (China). Other chemicals and reagents used in this study were of analytical grade or food grade unless stated otherwise. All strains, plasmids and primers used in this study are listed in Table S1.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Collection of plastic wastes from 20-year-old landfill
ce:section.ce:para: The waste plastic pieces with 10 × 10 cm in size were collected from a 20-year-old landfill located at Jinxian, Anhui province, China (N31°1’21’’, E119°7’48’’), taken from the landfill at a depth of 2 m. Picked samples were transferred to sterile 50 mL falcon tubes with an ice pack, which were used for the isolation of potential PU degrader.

The plastic wastes were incubated in liquid mineral salt medium for potential PU-degrading microbe isolation. Then the plastic wastes were washed with tap water for many times, and the attachments were picked out during the cleaning process. The clean plastic samples were washed six times with deionized water, followed by drying at 50 °C for 24 h for FTIR spectroscopy analysis (Thermo Scientific Nicolet iS20, USA).

ce:section.ce:section-title: Isolation and screening of PU-degrading microbes from plastic wastes
ce:section.ce:para: For microbe isolation, Impranil® DLN-SD (an anionic aliphatic polyester polyurethane dispersion (Covestro AG, Leverkusen, German) and chemosynthetic PBA-PU were utilized as the substrates to prepare opaque agar plates [10]. The PBA-PU or DLN agar plates containing 5% (v/v) LB or PDA were used for isolating bacterial or fungal strains. The collected waste plastic pieces with attached soil were incubated in liquid mineral salt medium for 24 h at 30 °C and 180 rpm with glass beads. Afterwards, the suspension was used for continuous gradient dilution and then spread on LB and PDA medium. The plates were incubated at 30 °C for 4–6 days. During incubation, microbes capable of growing on the PBA-PU and DLN agar plates with transparent zone were isolated and purified. The isolate G-9 with high transparent zone diameter was screened as candidate for further use.

18 S rRNA genes that code for 18 S ribosomal RNA are widely used in phylogenetic analysis. For identification of the potential PU-degrader, the genomic DNA of the isolate G-9 was extracted, and portion of the 18 S rRNA was amplified using the universal fungal primers NS1 (5′-GTAGTCATATGCTTGTCTC-3′) and NS4 (5′-CTTCCGTCAATTCCTTTAAG- 3′) [23]. The sequencing data of the PCR products were aligned and analyzed using the database of the National Biotechnology Information Center of the United States (NCBI, https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/). The phylogenetic tree was constructed by the Neighbor-Joining method (MEGA 7) [24].

For quantitative evaluation of PU degradation, strain G-9 was first cultivated in YPD medium (1% yeast extract, 2% tryptone, 2% glucose, w/v) at 28 °C for 2–3 days, and 200 μL cells (1 ×106 cells/mL) of strain G-9 were inoculated into 20 mL mineral salt medium with different addition of YPD medium (40%, 70%, 100%, v/v) and 0.2 g of autoclaved PU foam (3 ×1.5 ×0.5 cm3). The flasks were incubated in static culture at 30 °C for 15 days. Otherwise, 200 μL cells of strain G-9 were inoculated into 20 mL YPD medium with 0.2 g autoclaved PU foam, followed by cultivation at 30 °C for 7, 14 and 21 days, respectively. The cultivation without strain G-9 was used as control.

To measure the weight loss of plastics from different treatments, PU foams were recovered from culture and thoroughly washed with 0.5% (w/v) sodium hypochlorite solution to remove the adhering biomass and components of medium. After that, the foams were washed with sterilized water, dried at 60 °C to a constant weight. Weight loss was calculated using the formulae: weight loss = (initial weight-final weight) ∕ initial weight × 100%. The surface morphology of PU foam was observed by scanning electron microscope (SEM, Hitachi SU8010).

To explore the possible PU degradation products, 2 mL supernatant was collected from PU degradation with strain G-9 for 28-days or degrading enzyme for 2-days, and then the supernatant was freeze-dried for product identification. The dry powder was re-dissolved with methanol, and filtered through a 0.22-μm nylon membrane. The contained metabolites from degradation were analyzed by Thermo Scientific Q Exactive UHMR mass spectrometer (USA) under the referred operating parameters [10].

Strain G-9 was cultured in the MSM medium with 20% YPD medium and 0.2% Impranil DLN for 3 days, after which the supernatant was harvested by centrifugation at 10, 000g and 4 °C for 20 min. The esterase activity of the supernatant of strain G-9 was measured using p-nitrophenol butyrate (pNPB) as the substrate. Briefly, 1 mL reaction mixtures containing 10 μL supernatant or dilute enzyme and 10 μL pNPB (1 mM, final concentration) in 50 mM Tris-HCl buffer (pH 8.0) were incubated at 37 °C for 10 min. The activity was determined by measurement of the absorption at 410 nm (A410). One unit of esterase activity was defined as the amount of enzyme that releases 1 μmol p-nitrophenol per minute with p-nitrophenol as the standard. The protein concentration was determined by the Bradford method using bovine serum albumin (BSA) as the standard [25].

Measurement of enzyme activity with different p-nitrophenyl (pNP) esters was done as described before [26]. Using the pNP-butyrate (C4) as the optimal substrate, the effects of temperature and pH on esterase activity and stability of supernatant or degrading enzyme were determined [26]. All enzyme assays were performed in triplicate, and the activities shown are averages of the values from three independent experiments.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Purification and identification of PU-degrading enzyme from the supernatant of strain G-9
ce:section.ce:para: The supernatant of strain G-9 culture (SUP) from 3 days incubation was prepared as described above. For purification of PU-degrading enzyme, 2 L SUP was fractionated at 40% saturation ammonium sulfate in cold condition, followed by centrifugation at 12,000g and 4 °C for 20 min, and the pellet was then dissolved in 20 mL of 50 mM Tris-HCl buffer (pH 8.0) and dialyzed against the same buffer to remove the salt. The obtained protein fraction was fractionated by ion exchange chromatography (IEC) on a Capto Q column (GE Healthcare), eluted with a linear sodium chloride gradient using 50 mM Tris-HCl buffer (pH 8.0) and 50 mM Tris-HCl buffer containing 1 M NaCl (pH 8.0) at a flow rate of 2 mL/min. Fractions with esterase activity and PBA-PU degradation ability were collected and dialyzed, which were further purified by gel filtration chromatography (GFC) on a HiLoad 16/600 Superdex 200 pg column (GE Healthcare) with Tris-HCl buffer (50 mM, pH 8.0) at a flow rate of 1 mL/min. The active fractions were analyzed by SDS-PAGE.

After electrophoresis, the gel was cut into two strips for staining and zymogram analysis. One strip was stained normally, while SDS was removed from another gel strip for zymogram analysis by incubating the gel twice with 2.5% (vol/vol) Triton X-100. The gel was incubated in 0.1 M Tris-HCl (pH 8.0) and then in 50 mM Tris-HCl (pH 8.0) to renature the enzyme [27]. The renatured gel was incubated on a 1.5% agar plate containing 0.01% C4 and 0.1% PBA-PU (m/v) at 37 °C for 15 min and 5 h, respectively. The stained gel band corresponding to the location of the transparent and yellow zones from the zymogram analysis was excised and analyzed by NanoLC–ESI–MS/MS, the draft genome of strain G-9 (PRJNA1061465) was referred.

To evaluate the polyurethane degradation ability of the purified protein, degradation assay of PU foam was performed using the purified protein by changing the protein dosage (0–0.24 U/mg PU foam) and incubation time (0–48 h) in 2 mL Tris-HCl buffer (50 mM, pH 8.0). The weight of PU foam was 50 mg. During hydrolysis, the pH value was monitored to represent the production of degradation product. After degradation, the weight loss of foam was calculated, and the surface morphology was observed by SEM. Meantime, degradation of PBA-PU emulsion was performed in 200 μL Tris-HCl buffer (50 mM, pH 8.0) containing 0.1% PBA-PU and purified enzyme (30 U/mL), followed by incubation at 37 °C for 30 and 90 min, respectively.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Sequence analysis and structure prediction of PU-degrading enzyme
ce:section.ce:para: The enzyme was named as BaCut1. The domains of BaCut1 were predicted using the National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) database. The signal peptide was predicted using the SignalP 5.0 Server. The protein sequences and phylogenetic analysis of the reported esterase, cutinase and amidase was performed using ClustalW version 2.0 and MEGA 7 [24], respectively.

AlphaFold is a novel machine learning approach that incorporates physical and biological knowledge about protein structure, which is used to predict BaCut1’s 3D structure from its amino acid sequence [28]. The reference structure is the cutinase-like enzyme from phyllosphere yeast (7cw1). The substrate of representative model of PBA chain was optimized by the Gaussian 09 software [29] at B3LYP/6–31 G(d) level [30]. The docking experiment was performed with Autodock Tool 1.5.6 [31]. The oxygen atom of the Ser107 residue was set as the center of the grid box, and the grid point values of the X-, Y-, and Z-axes were set to 30, 30, and 30, respectively.

The gene encoding BaCut1 and its homologs were synthesized and inserted into pET29a (+) digested with EcoRI and XhoI to produce plasmid pET29a-BaCut1. For BaCut1D148A, BaCut1G38A, BaCut1E41A, BaCut1T47A, BaCut1Y106A, BaCut1I195A and BaCut1L200A, site-directed mutagenesis was applied using homologous recombination by amplification of the entire circular plasmid (Mut Express II Fast Mutagenesis Kit V2, Vazyme). The primers used for amplification are shown in Table S1. E. coli BL21 (DE3) was transformed with the plasmids to produce the recombination strains. The recombinant protein expression was induced by adding 0.2 mM isopropyl β-D-thiogalactoside (IPTG) to a final concertation 0.2 mM at 16 °C. The cells were harvested and sonicated in 50 mM Tris-HCl buffer (pH 8.0) after 24 h induction. The lysate was centrifuged at 12,000g for 20 min, and the supernatant was subjected to Ni Sepharose 6 Fast Flow column (GE Healthcare) to purify the His-tagged recombinant BaCut1 and its variants.

To evaluate the degradation ability of the purified recombinant protein, BaCut1 (50 μg/mL) was mixed with PU foam (25 mg), agricultural film PBAT (10 mg), PET (10 mg) and 25 mg PBA-PUR in 4 mL Tris-HCl buffer (50 mM, pH 8.0) at 30 °C for 48 h with continuous gentle stirring. After the reaction, the plastic was recovered and dried to constant weight, and the weight loss rate was calculated. To identify the enzyme dosage during degradation, BaCut1 (0.1 mg, 0.3 mg and 0.5 mg) was incubated with PU foam (25 mg) and PBAT (10 mg) in 4 mL Tris-HCl buffer (50 mM, pH 8.0) at 30 °C for 48 h with continuous gentle stirring. After treatment, the weight loss was calculated after drying, the surface morphology was observed using SEM, and the molecular weight was evaluated by Gel permeation chromatography (GPC) analysis (Agilent PL-GPC220, USA) [32]. The degradation products were analyzed by MS equipped with an electrospray ionization probe [10], and quantification of monomer adipic acid was performed by HPLC equipped with a C18 reverse-phase column (4.6 ×150 mm, 5 µm) [15]. Adipic acid was used as the standard. To compare the degradation capacity, BaCut1 and LCCICCG (50 μg/mL) were mixed with PU foam (25 mg) and PBAT (10 mg) in 4 mL Tris-HCl buffer (50 mM, pH 8.0). The mixture was incubated at different temperature (30 °C, 37 °C, 45 °C and 55 °C) for 48 h with continuous gentle stirring. The weight loss was calculated as described above. Otherwise, BaCut1 (1.6 nmol/mL, 50 mM Tris-HCl, pH 8.0, 37 ℃) or IsPETase (1.6 nmol/mL, 50 mM Glycine-NaOH buffer, pH 9.0, 30 ℃) were mixed with PU foam (25 mg) and PBAT (10 mg) in 5 mL reaction system for 48 h with continuous gentle stirring. The weight loss was calculated as described above.

Experiments involved in degradation test were repeated three times where consistent results were found. Data represent mean ± SE of all biological replicates. Statistical significance was assessed by one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) followed by Duncan’s test as a multiple comparison test using SPSS 20.0 (IBM Inc., Chicago, IL, USA). A value of p < 0.05 was considered statistically high significant (lowercase, like a, b, c).

ce:section.ce:section-title: PU-like plastic wastes in landfills exhibit signs of biodegradation
ce:section.ce:para: Incineration and landfilling are the most commonly employed strategies for managing solid waste plastic. Hence, we gathered plastic wastes samples from a 20-year-old landfill ( Fig. 1). According to their appearance (Fig. S1a) and highly consistent peak of FTIR peak profiles (Fig. S1b) compared to commercially available fruit packaging made of PU-plastic, we infer that the collected wastes primarily consist of PU plastics. To investigate their surface morphology and structural characteristics, we conducted thorough analyses. As shown in Fig. 1, the plastic wastes retrieved from the landfill exhibited a yellowish hue, their surfaces appeared rougher with signs of fracturing. Upon SEM examination, it was observed that one section (region R1) of a PU-like plastic waste exhibits a visible smooth surface, while another section (region R2) shows rougher topography with appeared layered. These observations indicate that the PU-like plastic wastes have undergone biodegradation during their extended exposure in the landfill environment. These findings underscore the potential role of landfills as habitats for soil microbes possessing the capability to degrade plastics.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Efficient PU-degradation by Blastobotrys sp. G-9 derived from plastic wastes
ce:section.ce:para: Given the evident signs of biodegradation in the collected PU-like plastic wastes, we next sought to identify the microbes involved in PU-degradation. Initially, 32 isolates were obtained using Impranil® DLN as the screening substrate, with only 6 isolates exhibiting growth on PBA-PU agar plate, accompanied by visible transparent zones (Fig S2a). Notably, the use of Impranil DLN® as a substrate for assessing, the PUR degrading ability yielded insufficiently representative of the common solid form of most PU waste, highlighting the suitability of PBA-PU as a screening substrate for the polyester plastic-degrading microbes. Among the isolates, strains G-9 and G-11 were identified as the excellent degrader based on the ratio of transparent zone diameter to colony diameter. Morphological observation and phylogenetic analysis revealed that isolate G-9 belongs to the genus Blastobotrys (designated as strain G-9) (Fig. S2b), while isolate G-11 was identified as a member of Amycolatopsis (data not shown). Additionally, our observations indicated that representative genera of Blastobotrys form two distinct branches in the phylogenetic tree, along with Aspergillus niger (Fig. S2b). Since Blastobotrys and Aspergillus have been previously reported to possess potential PU biodegradation capabilities [3], we hypothesize that these strains may share a common evolutionary path under the unique conditions of the 20-year-old landfill environment.

To further assess the degradation ability of isolated strains G-9 and G-11 toward commercial PU waste, PU foam (TDI-based) obtained from Dagong foam Co., Ltd (Nantong, China) were used as the substrate. After 15 days of cultivation, the weight loss of PU foam (Dagong foam Co., Ltd, Nantong, China) reached 34.8% and 50.2% in 70%-YPD and YPD rich medium, respectively, resulting in significantly shrinkage and collapsed of the PU foam's thickness and volume after yeast cell removal, compared to control group without strain G-9 inoculation ( Fig. 2a). In contrast, only 4.7% weight loss was observed in the strain G-11 treatment. Consequently, strain G-9 was utilized for following degradation assay.

The effects of nutrition on degradation revealed that PUR-degradation by strain G-9 is reliant on available nutrition, indicating its inability to thrive solely on plastic as the carbon source. To evaluate the effect of incubation time on PU-degradation, strain G-9 was incubated in YPD rich medium with 1% PU foam (w/v). After 7 days of cultivation, the weight loss of PU foam waste reached 41.0%, increasing to 68.1% after 21 days of incubation (Fig. 2b). Similar weight loss was observed after 14 and 21 days of incubation, suggesting the accessible properties of esterase toward the soft segments of PU, while hard segments comprising isocyanate groups and chain extender moieties remained highly resistant to enzymatic hydrolysis.

Moreover, the morphology of the PU foam was assessed following treatment with strain G-9. SEM observations revealed an abundance of yeast cells adhered to the surface of PU foam, accompanied by visible cracks and perforated structures, whereas the PU foam from control group exhibited a normal appearance (Fig. 2c). Blastobotrys adeninivorans predominantly grows as mycelia at high-temperature (>42 °C), while it adopts as budding cell morphology at lower temperature (<42 °C) [33]. However, only ovate cells of strain G-9 were observed adhering to the surface of PU foam, indicating that the cultured environment may not be conducive to its optimal growth. Throughout the degradation process of PU foam, intermediate metabolite adipic acid was detected, with molecular ions at m/z 145 (M-H) -, while the derivates of 4,4'-methylenedianiline (MDA) were not detected (Fig. S3). PU comprises segmented copolymers with soft segments (polyester- or polyether-based polyols) and structured hard segments consisting of the isocyanate groups and chain extender moieties [34]. Based on the detection of the metabolite adipic acid, we deduced that strain G-9 catalyzes the hydrolysis of the soft segment of PU foam through enzymatic hydrolysis of the ester bonds.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Purification and identification of a novel cutinase from strain G-9 for PU degradation
ce:section.ce:para: The identification of adipic acid from the 14 day-degradation of PU by strain G-9 (Fig. S3) prompted us to investigate the degradative activity of the supernatant of strain G-9 (SUP). To evaluate the activity of SUP, a piece of PU foam (50 mg) was inoculated in 100 mL SUP solution at 30 °C for 2 days, with heat-inactive SUP serving as control. SEM observations showed abundant degradation and a collapsed skeleton structure in the SUP-treated sample, along with cracks and perforated structures ( Fig. 3a), mirroring the effects observed with strain G-9. These results indicate that strain G-9 secretes enzymes t capable of degrading PU.

Subsequently, we next sought to identify the enzyme responsible for strain G-9 degradation, focusing on esterase in the SUP fraction due to its degradation of PU foam and PBA-PU. Biochemical assays revealed that SUP displays highest activity toward p-nitrophenol butyrate (C4) substrate at 37 °C and pH 8.0 (Fig. S4a-c). Esterase activity was utilized as an indicator to guide the protein purification process. Following ammonium sulfate fractional precipitation, ion exchange chromatography (IEC) on Hitrap capto Q and gel filtration chromatography (GFC) on HiLoad 16/600 superdex 200 pg (Fig. S4d), a protein with esterase activity (129.5 U/mg) and PBA-PU degradative ability was purified (Fig. S4e), as confirmed by zymogram analysis using pNPA and PBA-PU as the substrates (Fig. 3b). Distinct yellow bands and transparency resulting from hydrolysis of pNPA and PBA-PU were observed. To further verify the PUR-degradative ability of the purified enzyme, decomposition of the purified enzyme toward PBA-PU and PU-foam was evaluated. The purified enzyme decomposed emulsible PBA-PU solution into clear state (Fig. 3c), and the degradation of PU foam was time- and dose-dependent, creating an adipic acid-mediated acidifying environment (Fig. 3d, e). Approximately 12% of the PU foam was degraded in 36 h at 0.24 U/mg plastic (Fig. 3e). These findings suggest that the purified enzyme with esterase activity can degrade commercial PU foam.

The degrading enzyme was further identified by peptide mass fingerprinting using tryptic peptide fragments of the purified enzyme referring to the draft genome of strain G-9 (GenBank: PRJNA1061465). The sequence of the most abundant fragment matched a predicted cutinase in the strain G-9 genome (Table S2). To assess its potential PU-degradative ability, the protein was heterologously expressed in E. coli BL21 (DE3) without signal peptide (Fig. S5a). Its specific enzyme activity was determined to be 1621.9 U/mg using C4 as the substrate. This enzyme was designated as BaCut1. Subsequently, we confirmed the decomposition activity of BaCut1on a PBA-PU agar plate, observing a transparent zone (Fig. S5b). Thus, BaCut1was selected as the PU degrader for the subsequent tests.

For phylogenetic tree analysis, reported esterases from yeast and representative cutinases with PU degradative ability were selected. The result showed that members of cutinases from yeast form an independent branch (Branch 3), while BaCut1 (PP259091) shared relatively low sequence identity (<30%) with known PU- or PET-degrading enzymes (Branch 1, 2, 4–6) (Fig. S5c). Within Branch 3, BaCut1 shared approximately 80% sequence identity with cutinases Acut1, Acut2 and Acut3 from the yeast Arxula adeninivorans (now named as Blastobotrys adeninivorans), followed by 50% sequence identity with emulsified poly(butylene succinate-co-adipate) (PBSA)-degrading cutinases PaE and CLE from yeast Pseudozyma antarctica and Cryptococcus sp. S-2, respectively. These yeast cutinases were found to have polycaprolactone degradation activity and cutinolytic activity [26,35]. However, whether they possess a function for degrading non-biodegradable plastic remains unknown. Additionally, three of BaCut1with 71–85% sequence identity were found in the genome of strain G-9 with a cluster distribution (Fig. S5d), but no PBA activity was detected. Our results indicate that BaCut1from Blastobotrys sp. G-9 represents a novel plastic-degrading enzyme with a newly discovered PU degradation function, which could not be discovered by simple alignment without expression verification.

ce:section.ce:section-title: BaCut1 decomposes PU foam and PBAT via ester bond cleavage
ce:section.ce:para: To assess the potential application of BaCut1 in plastic depolymerization and resource utilization, we initially investigated the biochemical properties of recombinant PU-depolymerase. With C4 as the optimal substrate (Fig. S6a), BaCut1displayed the highest activity at 37 °C and pH 8.0–9.0 (Fig. S6b, c). Moreover, it retained over 40% residue activity within a temperature range of 20 to 50 °C (Fig. S6d) and a pH range of 7.0–9.0 (Fig. S6e). Under these optimal conditions, we evaluated the degradation of PU foam and agricultural PBAT film. BaCut1 exhibited dose-dependent degradation of both PU and PBAT. After 48 h at 37 ℃, BaCut1 degraded 50% of commercial PU foam with a 2% usage amount (w/w, enzyme/plastic), leaving some visible insolubles in solution ( Fig. 4a). SEM analysis showed significantly degraded and collapsed of skeleton structure of PU foam after treatments with BaCut1, along with abundant holes and fissures on the plastics surface (Fig. 4b). To further characterize the hydrolysis of the PU, GPC analysis was performed on the residual solid part of the films after incubation. BaCut1 degradation resulted in a significant and progressive reduction in the molecular weights, with Mn and Mw reduced by 41.9% and 10.7%, respectively (Fig. 4c-d). During the degradation process of PU foam, the degradation product adipic acid was determined based on the molecular ions at m/z 145.06 (M-H) - (Fig. 4e), corresponding with the G-9-meditaed PU foam degradation (Fig. S3). We inferred that the structural complexity (variability in monomers) and specific ester bond cleavage of BaCut1 result in the production of large number of additives and degradation products with low abundance, which are challenging to distinguish by primary mass spectrometry. These results indicate that BaCut1 from Blastobotrys sp. G-9 decomposes PU via ester bond cleavage.

To analyze the potential of BaCut1 in degrading agricultural plastic film, degradation tests were performed on commercial PBAT film exposed to 0.5 mg BaCut1. After 48 h of hydrolysis, 18% of PBAT film was also degraded by BaCut1 when used at a 5% usage, under the same reaction conditions as the PU test. The films exhibited increased brittleness and fragmentation following enzymatic hydrolysis ( Fig. 5a). Additionally, five major intermediates were detected via LC-MS, indicating the formation of different products through ester bond cleavage. Mass spectra collected in positive mode revealed m/z values at 147.06, 167.03, 219.12, 239.09, 347.17 and 367.12, corresponding to adipic acid, TPA, AB, BTa, ABA and ABTa, respectively (Fig. 5a, b). SEM observations showed clean surface and absence of fractures in untreated PBAT film, while treated film exhibited perforated structures and rough surfaces after BaCut1 treatment (Fig. 5c). These results demonstrate that BaCut1 is also able to degrade PBAT film into their monomeric constituents.

Given the high activity of BaCut1 at ambient temperature, we proposed that this enzyme could be utilized for enzymatic processing of polyester plastics, contributing to the potential of a circular plastic economy. Adipic acid, a key organic diacid intermediate in plastics manufacturing, has garnered commercial interest in bio-renewable routes for its production [36]. Therefore, we quantitatively determined the adipic acid monomers from BaCut1-mediated PU and PBAT depolymerization using HPLC and a commercial adipic acid-mediated standard curve. Adipic acid was recovered from the PU degradation solution with a yield of 43.9% using an 8% enzyme dosage at 37 °C for 24 h, while a 33.2% isolation yield with a purity of 53.5% was obtained from PBAT degradation ( Table 1). During to the complexity of structural components, the purity of released monomer from PU was not evaluated. These results indicate that BaCut1 holds potential for the biodegradation of PU and PBAT, providing a promising avenue for recovering the monomers from commercial polyester products.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Comparison of BaCut1 and LCC and PETase in polyester plastics depolymerization
ce:section.ce:para: Given the efficient depolymerization of PU foam and PBAT by cutinase enzyems, we compared the activity of LCCICCG (F243I/D238C/S283C/Y127G) [37], IsPETase [17] and BaCut1in hydrolyzing PU foam and PBAT at various temperature using commercial PU foam and PBAT film. BaCut1 outperformed LCCICCG at 37 and 45 °C during PU foam depolymerization, reaching a weight loss of 45% at 45 °C compared to 25% weight loss of LCCICCG ( Fig. 6a). Additionally, at the optimal catalytic temperature of 37 °C, BaCut1 outperformed LCCICCG in PBAT degradation, with a weight loss of 45%, compared to 30% weight loss of LCCICCG (Fig. 6b). Although LCCICCG demonstrates the highest thermostability with improved melting temperatures of 94 °C [37], and IsPETase can degrade PET at a moderate temperature (30 °C) [17]. We also compared BaCut1 with IsPETase. When compared to IsPETase, BaCut1 outperformed IsPETase during PU depolymerization at the optimum catalytic temperature, achieving a weight loss of approximately 30% compared to 13% weight loss of IsPETase (Fig. 6c). However, IsPETase showed better performance than BaCut1 in PBAT degradation. It's worth noting that, unlike LCC with its high PET-specific depolymerization rate, BaCut1 exhibited no activity toward PET.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Possible catalytic mechanism of BaCut1-mediated polymeric monomer accumulation
ce:section.ce:para: Compared to other esterases, cutinases display enhanced potency in PBAT decomposition by breaking the ester bond adjacent to phenyl residues, resulting in the dominant products BTa and TPA, akin to TfCut [15]. However, BaCut1 exhibited a distinct hydrolysis pattern, yield adipic acid as the primary product in both PU and PBAT breakdown, along with AB and ABA, alongside minor quantities of TPA, BTa and ABTa as per abundance analysis (Fig. 5b). The catalytic mechanism of BaCut1-mediated PU decomposition was further elucidated by structure modeling and molecular docking. Multiple sequence alignment showed that BaCut1 contains conserved G-Y-Q-G motif, which is representative characteristic of the α/β hydrolase superfamily (Fig. S7). To identify the key amino acids responsible for PU chain binding, we docked a repeat unit of PBA-PU to BaCut1 (Fig. S8). Conserved amino acids S107, D184, H199 were determined as the catalytic triad, with the PBA-PU model substrate fitting snugly within the active site of BaCut1 ( Fig. 7a, Fig. S7). Notably, the catalytic triad was close to the aliphatic part (Fig. 7a), which extended to fit within a cleft across, lined by amino acids such as E41, T47, Y106, I195 and L200. Other residues (e.g. Q76, L161, S162, and I195) in the active site of BaCut1 mainly interacted with the aromatic part of PBA-PU. Different residues (e.g. Y100, W195, and I218) in PBAT-degrading cutinase TfCut were responsible for binding the aromatic part [15].

To verify the involvement of specific amino acids, corresponding site-directed mutations were constructed. D184A, G38A, E41A, Y106A and T47A exhibited a significant decrease of esterase activity, followed by I195A and L200A (Fig. 7b). Together with the biochemical and structural analyses, we propose the potential mechanism of BaCut1 in PU binding and biodegradation. The binding conformation of PBA-PU model substrate implies that S107 is likely to attack the ester bond adjacent to the adipic acid-terminus, generating products such as adipic acid, AB and 1,4-butanediol. While most proposed products were experimentally identified, the absence of 1,4-butanediol release may be attributed to detection equipment limitations. BaCut1 recognizes PBA-PU by positioning the aliphatic chains within the hydrophobic substrate-binding pocket (G38, E41, Y106, I195, L200), as evidenced by decreased activity upon mutation of these residues to alanine. We propose that G38 and Y106 serve as the oxyanion hole and are essential for the catalytic process, supported by the nearly complete loss of degradation ability in G38A and Y106A variants towards PBA-PU (Fig. 7c, Fig. S7).

Accumulation of synthetic plastic waste in the environment has become a global concern. Compared to mechanical or chemical recycling, development of biodegradable plastics [38,39], or bio-recycling of plastic waste using renewable enzymes or microbes has become a desirable approach for plastic waste end-of-life processing [6,40]. Series of advanced achievements about engineered LCC or PETase with improved catalytic performance have proved the feasibility to advance PET plastics biodegradation [37,41,42]. The reported microbes and degrading enzymes capable of degrading PU polymers have proved the feasibility of biodegradation of PU plastics. However, degradation of PU into oligo- and monomeric compounds by PU-degrading enzymes is of fundamental importance for a circular plastic economy [43]. In this study, we identified a novel secretory cutinase BaCut1 from fungal strain Blastobotrys sp. G-9. BaCut1 could recognize PBA-PU by positing the aliphatic chains into hydrophobic substrate-binding pocket, and cleave the ester bond adjacent to the adipic acid-terminus, which provide new feasible route for PU plastic disposal in the future.

Fungi Cryptococcus, Aspergillus, Cladosporium and bacteria Bacillus, Pseudomonas and Acinetobacter have been identified to degrade PU foam or film with high weight loss [3,7]. Especially, Cladosporium sp. P7 could degrade polyester-PU foam waste with 15.3% and 83.8% weight loss in MSM and PDB medium [10]. These results indicates that fungi-mediated PU degradation may find superiority due to the robust growth and surface attachment accessing to hydrophobic plastic interface [44,45]. These characteristics are beneficial for fungal survival under nutrient-limited environment via long-term adaptation [7]. Compared to filamentous fungi, yeast strains degraded cutin and PCL by cutinase-like enzyme [26,35,46], which are regarded as potential industrial enzyme for chemical production [47]. Blastobotrys sp. G-9 was isolated from the degradative PU surface collected from a 20-year-old landfill, which displayed efficient surface adhesion toward PU foam. Strain G-9 caused visible cracks and perforated structures with 60% weight loss after 21 days treatment (Fig. 2). This surface colonization may promote PU decomposition by increasing the local enzyme concentration through ester bond breaking, and promoting the following enzymatic hydrolysis [48]. Our results show that yeast strain and secreted cutinases are potential resources for PU plastics biodegradation.

Degradation of PU plastics by microbes is mainly attributed to the enzymatic action of esterases, ureases, proteases and amidases, with adipic acid, butylene glycol, TPA and toluene diamine as the degradation products [49]. The plastics-active enzymes database (PAZy) representing an inventory of known and experimentally verified enzymes toward synthetic fossil fuel-based polymers is build [50]. Most of reported PU-degrading enzymes are PET-depolymerizing enzymes, such as LCC, Tcur0390 and Tcur1278. There enzymes commonly exhibit activity toward polyester PUR nanoparticles, hydrophilic polyurethane or highly pure PU without additives [19,20]. However, the used substrates cannot represent the commercial PU synthetic polymeric materials. BaCut1 from Blastobotrys sp. G-9 shared conserved catalytic sites but low sequence identity (<30%) with the well-known PU- or PET-degrading enzymes. BaCut1 demonstrated efficient degradation toward commercial polyester plastics PUR and agricultural film PBAT, while no activity was observed from PET. We deduced that BaCut1 is a specific PU degrading enzyme, which showed efficient PU and PBAT depolymerization at moderate temperature compared to engineered LCCICCG and IsPETase [17]. Cutinases Acut1, Acut2 and Acut3 from Blastobotrys share about 85%− 93% sequence identities with BaCut1. The three enzymes were active in a pH range of pH 4.5–6.5 and a temperature range of 20–30 °C, with short-chain fatty acid esters as the optimal substrate (C4 and C6) [26]. BaCut1 displays similar substrate specificity but higher temperature and pH optimum (pH 8.0, 37 °C) (Fig. S4). The three enzymes from Blastobotrys showed polycaprolactone degradation activity and cutinolytic activity, while its degradation of polyester plastic was not evaluated [26]. In the genome of strain G-9, three enzymes that shared high sequence identity with BaCut1 are present (Fig. S5d). However, the three homologous proteins exhibited esterase activity, but no PBA activity. These results show that cutinase BaCut1 possessing solid PU degradation activity exhibits unique sequence evolution features.

PU biodegradation is involved in adhesion and following hydrolysis, and enzymes implicated in PU biodegradation are either secreted, membrane-bound [51], or possible cell wall-associated ones. PU-surface-binding has been identified to be essential for PU degradation [52]. However, the surface or monomer-binding of solid waste PU restricts the efficient decomposition. In this situation, secretory degrading enzyme BaCut1 enabled efficient polymer degradation by possible cell adhesion with high enzyme-substrate contact (Fig. 2c). The grinding PU surface (Fig. 3a) may provide contact interface for the degrader. Our results prove that free degrading enzymes released directly into the medium are efficient for PU degradation by local cells adhesion. The binding of PBA-PU in the active site of BaCut1 implies that BaCut1 is more likely to attack the ester bond adjacent to the adipic acid-terminus, generating products such as adipic acid, AB and 1,4-butanediol. Most proposed products were experimentally identified, except for 1,4-butanediol. We speculate that the absence of 1,4-butanediol release may due to the limitations of detection equipment.

Biodegradation provides a way for resource utilization of waste plastic. PET degradation products terephthalic acid and ethylene glycol can be converted into PET or PBA [6,53], which could be borrowed to advance sustainable use of PU and PBAT wastes. However, PU or PBAT polymers have a more complex backbone compared to PET [22,54]. Hence, conversion of the mixed products into high-value compounds is limited. As an efficient PU degrader, BaCut1 hydrolyzed PU into adipic acid with 43.9% recovery. During the degradation, a special aliphatic part-binding feather was observed, which may be the key characteristic leading to the special hydrolysis of PU. Since adipic acid is a key organic diacid intermediate used in nylon manufacturing [55], hydrolysis of PU into adipic acid by BaCut1 should possess higher application potential in the plastic circular economy. Our findings provide the primary understanding of effective enzyme mediated PU-degradation, which will facilitate further enzyme engineering to advance the development of PU biodegradation in the future.

Efficient bio-biodegradation and recycling of waste plastics is highly desirable as PU is widely used and increasingly accumulates in the environment. PU-depolymerizing enzymes could degrade PU into monomeric components, which serve as ingredient for synthesizing new materials. Hence, these enzymes are considered as the critical catalyst for plastic disposal. In the present study, a novel cutinase BaCut1 was identified from Blastobotrys sp. G-9 with the ability to degrade PU and PBAT. At 37 ℃ for 48 h, BaCut1 could degrade commercial polyester plastics PU foam with 50% and 18% weight loss, respectively. During the hydrolysis, adipic acid was released as the major end-product by a special PBA chain-binding feature. However, more effects are needed to improve the catalytic rate of depolymerase BaCut1 with the aim to realize the open-loop recycling and upcycling of plastic wastes.

Environmental pollution caused by plastic waste has become global problems that needs to be considered urgently. About 79% of the waste plastic (6.3 billion tonnes in 2015) that ended up in landfills or natural environment is threatening our ecological environment and potentially the safety of our entire food system. Polyurethane (PU) contains soft segments (long polyester- or polyether-based polyols) and organized hard segments (polyisocynates). Compared to these traditional PUR waste disposal methods, recycling is a much more desirable approach for PUR end-of-life processing. In recent years, biodegradation using microorganisms or enzymes has become a promising alternative for plastic recycling. However, the complex structures of PUR are highly resistant to the bio-degradation, resulting in limited degradation efficiency of yet reported degradative microbes or enzymes. Hence, development of effective biodegradation and recycling process for PUR waste by efficient degradative enzyme is beneficial feature for the future recycling economy.
